conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You're here after your bronchoscopy with balloon dilation. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hey, doc. I’m okay, just some soreness in my throat and around the trach site. Expected that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. The team said you tolerated the procedure well. No breathing issues. You got Decadron during the procedure to reduce swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. Was the biopsy part okay? Any immediate findings?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy was successful. No results yet — that takes a few days. Main goal was to open up the narrowed area and get tissue to check for inflammation or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I’ve had Klebsiella and Pseudomonas before — hope it’s not back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching for that. Your sputum cultures from past episodes showed those, but no signs of infection now — no fever or increased secretions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. What about the chest X-ray they did earlier?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No pneumothorax, which is great. Heart size a bit enlarged, but stable. Lungs clear. So, no complications from the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely just a couple of days. We’re keeping you for pain control and monitoring. You’re on 6L oxygen via trach mask, and your saturation is 99% — excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. The oxycodone helped last time. Can I take it again if the pain flares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve ordered oxycodone 5mg every 6 hours as needed. We’ll also give acetaminophen regularly to help reduce the opioid dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate that. Any changes to my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No — you’re continuing your usual meds: methotrexate, prednisone, famotidine, and inhaled tobramycin. We’re keeping everything consistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Mr. ___. How’d you sleep? Pain under control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Slept okay. Took oxycodone once last night. Still some soreness, but manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your labs this morning show a high white count — 20.3 — but that’s likely from inflammation, not infection. Neutrophils are up, which fits with recent procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? Should we be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. No fever, lungs are clear, and you’re feeling stable. We’ll keep an eye on it, but it’s common after interventions like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. Any update on the second chest X-ray?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Done this morning — shows stable heart and lungs. No new fluid or collapse. Everything looks unchanged, which is what we want post-procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. I’ve had so many dilations — six just last year — but this one feels smoother.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the team noted good airway patency after dilation. We’ll keep following with interventional pulmonology. They’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Nurse said you had a little more bloody discharge from the trach — is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, usually happens for a day or two after dilation. It’s not heavy, just a bit more mucoid and tinged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. As long as it’s not increasing or bright red, we’re not concerned. Keep the site clean and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Any word from rheumatology or infectious disease?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ve been consulted. Rheumatology will follow up to manage your polychondritis. ID wants to review the biopsy and prior cultures, especially with your history of resistant organisms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I know my case is complex with the SMAD4 mutation and all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is, but we’re coordinating care. You’re doing well — no respiratory distress, walking independently, eating normally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow if all goes well. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Only took Tylenol this morning. Oxycodone not needed yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll send you home with a small supply of oxycodone — 10 tablets — just in case. But try to stick with Tylenol if you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the max for Tylenol again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No more than 3 grams a day — that’s six 500mg tablets. You’re on 650mg twice daily now, so stay on that schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any restrictions on activity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No heavy lifting for a week. Otherwise, resume normal activities as tolerated. Watch for increased pain, fever, or breathing trouble — call us if those happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-ups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes — interventional pulmonology, rheumatology, and infectious disease all have appointments scheduled. We’ll send you the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning! You’re cleared for discharge. We’re just waiting on your transport.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Everything set with meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes — same as before, but oxycodone is now 7.5mg every 4 hours as needed. Only take it if Tylenol isn’t enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And prednisone — do I taper?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No — you’re staying on 7.5mg daily. This is a maintenance dose for your condition, not a short-term taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Have a good one, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Nurse will be in shortly with discharge papers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Ready to get home.
